title: Condensate and diluent watch
dek: The other half of every Western Canadian Select (WCS) barrel: what diluent is, where Alberta's condensate comes from, the structural import shortfall, and the cost it puts on the heavy barrel.

claims.text: Dilbit is bitumen diluted with natural gas condensate, typically 30 to 35% by volume. It accounts for about 60% of all marketable crude production from the oil sands, and with the exception of the Kearl and Fort Hills mines, all of it comes from thermal in situ facilities.

Bitumen is extra heavy and almost solid at room temperature. Undiluted bitumen is non-marketable because it cannot be stored or shipped by pipeline, so it must be upgraded or diluted with a lighter hydrocarbon.

Alberta pipeline specifications require crude under 350 centistokes of viscosity and density under 940 kilograms per cubic metre (above 18.9 American Petroleum Institute (API) gravity). Condensate at 30% by volume or more is added to bitumen to meet that spec, producing dilbit.

Imperial Oil's investor materials define WCS, the Canadian heavy benchmark, as about one-quarter diluent and three-quarters bitumen, and the bitumen realization bridge backs the diluent cost out of the WCS price. Diluent is not a footnote, it is a line item in the netback.
claims.source: Imperial Oil investor presentation (via US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing)

claims.text: In 2024, Alberta pentanes plus production averaged 396.2 thousand barrels per day, up 6.8% year on year on higher recovery at field plants. Alberta demand reached 751.1 thousand barrels per day, up 5.1%, driven by higher bitumen production. The province consumed nearly twice what it produced.
claims.source: Alberta Energy Regulator, ST98 2025 (Alberta Energy Outlook)

claims.text: The AER's base-case forecast has pentanes plus production growing to 471.5 thousand barrels per day by 2034 while demand reaches 933.7 thousand barrels per day. Imports of pentanes plus into Alberta are expected to increase over the forecast period to cover the widening shortfall.
claims.source: Alberta Energy Regulator, ST98 2025 (Alberta Energy Outlook)

claims.text: The Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin (WCSB) imports roughly 260,000 barrels per day of condensate from the US to meet demand. Canada produces about 570,000 barrels per day of condensate, primarily from Montney and Duvernay unconventional plays, with the balance imported by pipeline.
Almost all of Western Canada's refined petroleum product imports from the US are condensate, which is used to blend with heavy bitumen so the blended bitumen can move by pipeline.
claims.source: Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers (CAPP), Canadian Refining Industry deck

claims.text: Imperial Oil's Q2 2026 MD&A says first-half average bitumen realizations rose $11.41/bbl year over year on higher marker prices, but that the gain was 'partially offset by a weaker WTI/WCS spread and higher diluent costs,' a concrete producer-level read that the diluent line item bit into netbacks even in a stronger tape. Its six-month averages: WTI US$82.77 (vs 67.52 in 2025), WCS US$68.19 (vs 56.25), WTI/WCS spread US$14.58 (vs 11.27), bitumen US$81.91 (vs 70.50), synthetic crude US$118.86 (vs 93.14).

Condensate is a premium light stream: Oil Sands Magazine notes that condensate and synthetic crude produced through bitumen upgrading can trade close to par or even at a small premium to West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the US benchmark.

Enverus Intelligence Research expects condensate prices to stay robust as oil sands growth lifts in-basin demand, a tailwind for producers with exposure to the liquids-rich Montney and Duvernay and for select midstreamers.

The arithmetic is unforgiving: every dilbit barrel carries about 30% condensate priced near WTI while the blended barrel sells at a heavy discount to WTI. When the condensate premium firms, bitumen producers absorb the cost, not refiners.
claims.source: Oil Sands Magazine (differentials page); Imperial Oil realization bridge (SEC filing)

claims.text: Gibson Energy's December 2025 Investor Day presentation targets 1 to 2 additional diluent recovery unit (DRU) phases, each with 50,000-plus b/d of capacity, entering service from 2028 onward, as part of a plan to deploy up to C$1 billion of growth capital over five years. That timeline matches the DRU expansion Rystad Energy cites as the main cover for the basin's projected condensate shortfall. A counter-note: a GuruFocus summary of Gibson's Q2 2026 earnings call said DRU expansion discussions had quieted, suggesting the timeline could slip.

Follow-up reporting on FTAI Energy Partners' Sep 28 agreement for the Port Arthur terminal and a 50% stake in the Hardisty diluent recovery unit sharpened the terms: Hydrocarbon Engineering reports FTAI expects the assets to generate about US$50 million of annual EBITDA over the next 12 months, with closing expected in Q4 2026 subject to regulatory approvals. TipRanks reports the deal was signed Sep 27 and will be financed by assuming roughly US$190 million of existing term debt plus a US$72 million Barclays acquisition facility, backed by a long-term take-or-pay contract with an investment-grade producer.

Pembina reported higher interruptible volumes on the Cochin condensate import pipeline in Q1 2026, attributing them to 'wider condensate price differentials,' alongside what it called favorable commodity prices and spreads across its pipeline systems. The company reported Q1 adjusted EBITDA of $1,131 million, down 3% year over year, while raising full-year 2026 guidance to $4.35-4.55 billion on stronger commodity prices.
claims.source: Pembina Pipeline Corporation (Q1 2026 results, via SEC 6-K)

claims.text: On its Q2 2026 earnings call, Enbridge liquids chief Colin Gruending said the company has 'a full value chain to import condensate on Southern Lights and Norlite with meaningful headroom on both assets prior to looping,' and that Southern Lights recently moved from cost-of-service to a contract model with upward-tilted returns and inflators, per GuruFocus's call summary. Gruending added that domestic condensate supply will be insufficient and more imports will be required as the basin grows, with Enbridge prepared to add import solutions.
claims.vintage: Enbridge Q2 2026 earnings call, Jul 31, 2026; accessed 2026-10-05

claims.text: FTAI Energy Partners, the midstream arm of FTAI Infrastructure, has agreed to buy the Port Arthur crude terminal in Texas and a 50 percent stake in the Diluent Recovery Unit (DRU) at Hardisty, Alberta, from USD Group. Diluent Recovery Units strip diluent from diluted bitumen so the condensate can be recycled back into Alberta's diluent pool rather than being exported with the barrel, which reduces the basin's structural reliance on imported diluent. The cash consideration is about 255 million US dollars, with closing expected in the fourth quarter of 2026 pending regulatory approvals; the release does not disclose the DRU's throughput capacity.

Two pipelines carry US condensate into the WCSB: Pembina's Cochin (design capacity 110,000 barrels per day; the Canada Energy Regulator (CER) available-capacity series at Fort Saskatchewan has printed 110,000 b/d since March 2018) and Enbridge's Southern Lights (nameplate 180,000 barrels per day; available capacity 198,000 barrels per day since the Line 13 Expansion entered service in July 2025; 165,000 barrels per day committed through 2030 under the 2023 open season). Both run at or near full: Southern Lights throughput reached 189,000 barrels per day in the third quarter of 2025, and Cochin throughput printed above its 110,000 b/d available capacity in several months of 2026.
claims.vintage: CER series through December 2025 (Southern Lights) and June 2026 (Cochin); accessed 2026-10-17
claims.source: Canada Energy Regulator (CER) throughput and capacity data; Enbridge Q4 2023 release (February 2024); Pembina (August 2019)

claims.text: Enbridge's Line 13 Expansion of Southern Lights entered service in July 2025, lifting the line's available capacity by about 10 percent to 198,000 barrels per day (31,500 cubic metres per day). Enbridge announced the program in February 2025 as a 15,000 barrel-per-day increment on the 180,000 barrel-per-day nameplate, part of its broader Mainline and regional system optimization program.
claims.vintage: Announced February 2025; in service July 2025; accessed 2026-10-17
claims.source: Enbridge; Canada Energy Regulator (CER) Line 13 Expansion project filing

claims.text: Diluent recovery units (DRUs) would recycle diluent at Edmonton rail terminals instead of importing it. Cenovus studied a unit to process 180,000 barrels per day of dilbit and recover 60,000 barrels per day of diluent for return to northern Alberta projects, at an estimated cost of $800 million to $1 billion. Imperial Oil ruled a DRU out for now, citing high cost and market uncertainty.

Eight Capital's analysis at the time estimated that DRUs at rail-loading terminals could free about one-third of each railcar's space and add roughly 190,000 barrels per day of incremental bitumen capacity if applied across 600,000 barrels per day of crude-by-rail. No major DRU has been built since.

The Hub's Oct 14 analysis, 'A missing ingredient in Canada's pipeline plans,' put the diluent constraint on Canada's pipeline ambitions in AER numbers: Alberta consumed about 781,300 barrels per day of pentanes plus in 2025 while producing just 424,600 barrels per day, a supply gap of roughly 357,000 barrels per day, and the Alberta Energy Regulator expects pentanes plus demand to approach 934,000 barrels per day by 2034. S&P Global's Kevin Birn put total Western Canadian diluent consumption, including condensate and other lighter hydrocarbons, at nearly 900,000 barrels per day. At a typical blend of about 30 percent diluent, a fully utilized 1 million barrel per day dilbit pipeline would alone move roughly 300,000 barrels per day of diluent.

In Rystad Energy's high case, building the proposed Alberta-to-British Columbia (AB-BC) pipeline alongside further Enbridge Mainline expansions (phases 3 and 4) pushes the implied condensate shortfall to about 383,000 b/d at 85% throughput utilization, which Rystad says domestic supply is unlikely to meet without additional natural gas egress. As costly alternatives, Rystad flags condensate imports by rail or using synthetic crude oil (SCO) as diluent, warning both could weigh on bitumen netbacks depending on future oil prices.
claims.vintage: Rystad Energy scenario analysis carried by OilPrice.com; accessed 2026-10-12

claims.text: Rystad Energy's scenario work on OilPrice.com puts numbers on the condensate question: its base case sees 840,000 b/d of additional Western Canadian egress built within the decade, which would need about 214,200 b/d of additional condensate for transport at 85% throughput utilization. Forecast domestic condensate supply growth of about 150,000 b/d leaves a gap of roughly 64,200 b/d, which Rystad says incremental Southern Lights capacity (15,000 b/d) and diluent recovery unit (DRU) expansion (50,000 to 100,000 b/d) can cover, leaving the condensate market tightly balanced.
claims.vintage: Rystad Energy scenario analysis carried by OilPrice.com; accessed 2026-10-12

claims.text: Enverus estimates non-upgraded Canadian oil sands production rises by about 100,000 barrels per day per year through 2028, which drives in-basin condensate demand higher each year. The highest-yielding condensate regions of the Montney in BC and Alberta cannot grow fast enough, so a supply gap becomes apparent within a couple of years.

There is a trade-off: the condensate-directed drilling that feeds the diluent pool also produces associated natural gas, which puts downward pressure on Alberta Energy Company (AECO) gas hub prices. Robust condensate demand is good for liquids-rich producers and bad for dry-gas producers.

Monthly tracking: the AER publishes in situ oil sands production volumes in ST53 and broader oil sands production, supply, and disposition in ST39, both monthly. The annual ST98 outlook is where the condensate supply and demand balance is formally reconciled.
claims.source: Alberta Energy Regulator (ST53 and ST39 statistical reports)
